title: New York Woman Pleads Guilty in Smuggling Ring That Brought Indians Across Canada Border
excerpt: Janet Terrance of Hogansburg admitted her role in a conspiracy that smuggled Indian and Romanian nationals into the U.S. via the Akwesasne Mohawk reservation, an operation that killed a family of four.
body:
• Janet Terrance, 45, of Hogansburg, New York, pleaded guilty for her role in a smuggling conspiracy that transported Indian and Romanian nationals across the U.S.-Canada border for profit.
  • The ring operated through the Akwesasne Mohawk reservation spanning the border, using vehicles and boats to move migrants in dangerous conditions.
  • A Romanian family of four, including two children under age three, drowned in the St. Lawrence River after their boat capsized during a smuggling attempt in March 2023.
  • Six conspirators have been identified; most have entered guilty pleas, with the alleged ringleader extradited from Canada.

A New York woman has pleaded guilty for her role in a human smuggling conspiracy that regularly transported Indian and Romanian nationals across the U.S.-Canada border for profit, a scheme that resulted in the deaths of a family of four in the St. Lawrence River.

Janet Terrance, 45, of Hogansburg, New York, admitted to conspiring with at least five others to bring foreign nationals into the United States for private financial gain, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

A Deadly Operation on the Northern Border

The smuggling ring operated through the Akwesasne Mohawk Indian Reservation, a territory that spans the U.S.-Canada border across parts of New York, Ontario, and Quebec. The group used vehicles and boats to transport migrants across the St. Lawrence River and through rural border areas.

https://x.com/PTI_News/status/2087358743357079620

"The defendant and her coconspirators — fueled by greed, indifference, and recklessness — smuggled aliens via vehicle and boat across the U.S.-Canada border in dangerous weather conditions."

— Antoinette T. Bacon, Justice Department Criminal Division

The conspiracy turned deadly on the night of March 29, 2023, when a Romanian family of four — a mother, father, a one-year-old boy, and a two-year-old girl — was put into a small boat to cross the St. Lawrence River despite freezing temperatures, strong winds, and poor visibility. The boat capsized, killing all four family members and the boat driver.

Prosecutors said the smugglers moved forward with the crossing despite one co-conspirator refusing to assist because of the dangerous weather conditions that night.

Six Conspirators, Multiple Guilty Pleas

Terrance faces up to 15 years in prison. She is one of six people charged in the operation. Co-conspirators Dakota Montour, 31, and Kawisiiostha Celecia Sharrow, 43, both of the Akwesasne Mohawk reservation in New York, entered guilty pleas in early 2025 and late 2024, respectively. Montour faces a potential life sentence.

Rahsontanohstha Delormier, 31, a dual Canadian-American citizen who served as a boat driver in the operation, was extradited from Canada and pleaded guilty in late June 2026. He faces up to 15 years in prison.

The alleged ringleader, Stephanie Square, 53, was also extradited from Canada in 2025 and pleaded guilty in late July 2026. Prosecutors said Square led the smuggling organization and recruited co-conspirators for specific crossings. A sixth co-conspirator, Timothy Oakes, 35, was arrested and awaits trial.

A Hub for Cross-Border Smuggling

The Akwesasne reservation has long been identified by federal authorities as a vulnerable corridor for cross-border smuggling. The territory's geography — straddling the international boundary with multiple river crossings and limited surveillance — makes it attractive to smuggling operations.

Acting U.S. Attorney Daniel Hanlon for the Northern District of New York called the case a reminder of the deadly consequences of border smuggling.

"A family of four died because a smuggling organization put them in harm's way for profit. Our top priority is the prosecution and dismantling of smuggling organizations."

— Daniel Hanlon, Acting U.S. Attorney, Northern District of New York

Indian Nationals Among Those Smuggled

While the family that perished was Romanian, court documents confirm that the conspiracy also smuggled Indian nationals across the border. The case is one of several in recent years highlighting the northern border as a route for Indians attempting to enter the U.S. illegally, often after first reaching Canada.

Federal authorities have prosecuted multiple smuggling operations along the U.S.-Canada border involving Indian migrants in recent years. In a separate case, Stacey Taylor, 42, of Plattsburgh, New York, was indicted for conspiring to smuggle primarily Indian nationals across the border after U.S. Border Patrol agents found three Indian citizens and one Canadian national in her vehicle near the Quebec border.

What's Next

Sentencing dates for Terrance and other co-conspirators have not been publicly announced. The investigation was led by Homeland Security Investigations with assistance from U.S. Border Patrol, Customs and Border Protection, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and the Akwesasne Mohawk Police Service. The Justice Department's Office of International Affairs secured the extraditions from Canada.
nri_angle: The case directly involves Indian nationals who were smuggled across the U.S.-Canada border, highlighting the dangerous and sometimes deadly routes some migrants take to enter the United States.
